summary: Examines long-term trends in the Internet's BGP routing table and the operational practices and protocol features behind them. It discusses how these affect the ability of inter-domain routing to scale. It is informational.

eli5.summary: The Internet's map keeps getting bigger and messier. This looks at why, and at what that means for whether routers can keep up.

questions: why is the routing table growing
subtitle: Analysis of BGP routing table growth and the scaling implications for inter-domain routing.

tldr.problem: The Internet's BGP routing table is growing explosively with changing characteristics: shift from hierarchy-based CIDR aggregation to fine-grained multi-homed networks and dense interconnection meshes, raising concerns about the scalability of current routing systems.
tldr.mechanism: The document analyzes 13 years of BGP table measurements identifying growth phases (pre-CIDR exponential, CIDR deployment plateau, CIDR growth, and current compound growth at 42% per year), examining contributing factors like multi-homing, traffic engineering via BGP, and lack of uniform operational practices.
tldr.outcome: Highlights the need for scalable inter-domain routing architectures and operational practices, and identifies areas for research into extensions or replacements to BGP that can handle millions of small routing entries.

today: RFC 3221 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted. It remains highly relevant for understanding inter-domain routing scalability challenges. The trends it identified have continued, with the routing table further fragmenting. The work on improving BGP scalability has been active, including research into new routing architectures and continued evolution of BGP itself through extensions like route filtering and more sophisticated path selection.

sections.title: Routing Growth and Scalability Concerns
sections.content:
As the Internet grows, the BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) routing table—which lists how to reach every network on the Internet—must expand to accommodate new networks and policies. This growth is not merely a matter of size; it affects convergence time when routes fail, the stability of routing announcements, and the granularity of traffic engineering control that networks can exercise.

The document examines trends visible in BGP table measurements spanning from 1988 to 2001, identifying how operational practices and protocol features contribute to routing table growth. Key findings include that AS (Autonomous System) numbers are growing at 51% per year, and the BGP table itself is growing at 42% per year as of 1998-2000, signaling a fundamental shift in how the Internet is being operated.
sections.eli5: The address map is growing much faster than anyone expected, and it's changing shape. Instead of tidy groups, there are millions of small entries being added all the time.

sections.title: Four Phases of BGP Growth
sections.content:
Pre-CIDR era (1988-1994): The routing table exhibited exponential growth, doubling approximately every year. Without intervention, this growth would have exhausted available router memory within a few years. The problem was driven by the Class A/B/C addressing scheme, which forced the network to create one routing entry per network, leading to explosive growth in the number of separate prefixes.

CIDR deployment (1994-1995): The introduction of Classless Inter-Domain Routing allowed providers to aggregate customer networks into single routing announcements, keeping the table stable at roughly 20,000 entries through 1994. This demonstrated that hierarchical address allocation could dampen growth.

CIDR growth phase (1998-1998): For the next four years until late 1998, the routing table grew at a linear rate of approximately 10,000 entries per year. Short-term instability in the routing system also decreased as aggregate routes absorbed edge-network instability. Route flap damping was very effective during this period.

Current growth phase (1998-2001): From late 1998 onward, the growth trend changed radically to compound growth at 42% per year, indicating that hierarchical routing aggregation is no longer effectively containing growth. This shift appears driven by multi-homing of small networks, increasing prevalence of traffic engineering via BGP, and a denser interconnection mesh between networks.
sections.eli5: At first routing exploded. Then people fixed it with grouping. That worked for a few years. But then companies started breaking it apart again for reliability and performance.

sections.title: Analysis of Growth Drivers
sections.content:
Multi-homed small networks: Small networks (often announced as a single /24 prefix) are increasingly multi-homed to multiple providers or peers. Multi-homing is seen as a substitute for upstream provider resiliency, with small networks becoming responsible for their own reliability rather than relying on provider redundancy. This creates an incentive to announce small, specific prefixes from each connection to enable rapid failover.

Traffic engineering via BGP: Networks use selective announcement of smaller address prefixes along different paths to balance traffic across multiple connections. Since BGP is the only inter-provider traffic engineering tool widely available, this practice places increasingly fine-grained prefixes into the global routing table. The granularity of table entries has declined from an average /18.0 in late 1999 to /18.6 by September 2001, corresponding to a shift from 16,000 to 10,700 individual addresses per routing entry on average.

Aggregation and holes: More than 55% of routing entries (approximately 59,000 entries) are punching 'holes' in provider aggregates with more specific announcements. Of these, about 42,000 use distinct AS paths, indicating policy differentiation rather than simple load balancing. This evidence points to increasingly dense interconnection meshes where networks adopt multi-homed topologies without hierarchical structure.
sections.eli5: Small companies connect to multiple providers for backup. Companies also split up their addresses to control exactly how traffic flows to them. Both of these create millions of small entries instead of thousands of big ones.

sections.title: Requirements for Scalable Routing
sections.content:
Any future inter-domain routing system should support scalability at least two orders of magnitude larger than the current environment. Beyond sheer size, the system must exhibit stability (convergence to a consistent state and maintenance of that state when conditions are constant) and predictability (identical environmental conditions yield identical routing state).

Convergence time is a particular concern. Current BGP convergence following a route withdrawal takes approximately two minutes, which is slow for many modern applications. Faster convergence (on the order of seconds or less) would be desirable, though full sub-second convergence may not be practical.

The routing system must minimize overhead—the volume and frequency of routing protocol messages must be low enough that routers can afford to compute and handle route updates while maintaining an accurate view of network topology.
sections.eli5: The new system should handle way more routes without breaking. It should recover faster when connections fail. And it should use less bandwidth for routing messages.

sections.title: Possible Architectural Solutions
sections.content:
Several approaches are under consideration: extending BGP with new transitive route attributes to give originators more control over route propagation scope and policy; replacing BGP with a link-state protocol that broadcasts topologies and policies to all routers in a domain; or using overlay protocols on top of BGP to separate connectivity maintenance from traffic engineering and policy negotiation.

A critical architectural decision is policy opaqueness versus transparency. BGP uses distance vector routing where local policies are opaque—neighbors do not see exactly what decisions another network makes. Link-state protocols require policy transparency because all networks must announce their policies. In the inter-domain environment, many policies are proprietary and not publicly disclosed for business reasons, which may favor distance vector approaches.

Other possible refinements include proxy aggregation of grouped routing entries, definition of route attributes that specify propagation scope boundaries, and investigation of hierarchical routing models with more sophisticated aggregation mechanisms. The document raises the possibility of decoupling connectivity maintenance (link-state based), policy negotiation (overlay protocol), and traffic engineering (separate overlay) into distinct functional components that each scale better independently.
sections.eli5: The solution might extend BGP with more knobs, replace it with a different algorithm, or layer multiple protocols on top of each other. Each approach has different trade-offs.
